newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - Jobs data fail to alter views on Fed.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Jobs data fail to alter views on Fed.

text.p: Monetary policy prognosticators are split over how to interpret the tea leaves of Friday's robust U.S. jobs report, according to a Reuters survey of U.S. economists.
Experts had hoped the employment data would foreshadow the Fed's next move, but the report prompted few economists to change projections formulated earlier this week.
"This morning's data, rather than clarifying anything, seemed to muddy the waters," said Carol Stone, senior economist at Nomura Securities International Inc.

Sixteen of 30 economists said the Federal Reserve is likely to raise short-term interest rates at its September 24 policy meeting, unchanged from a Reuters survey conducted Tuesday and Wednesday. Six respondents do not expect a rate hike until the November 13 meeting, and one called for a tightening early next year. Five experts projected no move in 1996 and one forecast an ease in February of 1997.

The Labor Department reported Friday that the economy created 250,000 new jobs in August compared with 228,000 new jobs in July. The August unemployment rate dipped to 5.1 percent from 5.4 percent in July.

Many experts projecting a September 24 credit tightening said the jobs data confirmed their view. But those projecting a further-off tightening or no move in the foreseeable future also said Friday's data supported their views.

"Strong growth in employment, drop in the unemployment rate, rise in the workweek, large increase in average hourly earnings ... I regard it as a coherent picture of a tight and tightening labor market," said Charles Lieberman, chief economist at Chase Securities Inc who expects a 25-basis-point rate hike on Sept. 24.

On the other hand, "The Labor Department flags the fact that some of the summer strength in jobs comes from local education employment, and they think they're missing something in the seasonal adjustments," noted David Munro, chief U.S. economist at High Frequency Economics Inc.
Munro expects no Fed move in 1996 but said upcoming data could change his outlook.
"What matters is whether we get another Beige Book like the one we got last month, which suggested moderation (and) an absence of inflationary pressures in products," Munro said.
The Federal Reserve's Beige Book, a survey of economic conditions in each of the Fed's 12 regions, is scheduled for release next Wednesday.
